turn_text: I know that you started to get into this line of work as an intern with Senator George McGovern of South Dakota, who I know is not related to you, but also was the 1972 presidential nominee. How has the issue of food insecurity evolved over those years?

George McGovern got interested in this issue after watching a documentary on CBS back in the late 1960s called Hunger in America. And he was watching with his family and there was a scene of a young kid in school who didn't have anything to eat and the reporter asked the young boy, what's wrong? He says, I don't have any to eat and I'm ashamed. And George McGovern said, well, it's me, a United States senator, we should be ashamed that we would tolerate a system that would allow a little boy to be hungry in school. And so he helped form a special select committee on nutrition and human needs that he and other senators like Bob Dole, Republican, they did hearings all around the country exposing the problem of hunger. And then that led to a White House conference on food and nutrition that paved the way to expand the the Food Stamp Program, now known as SNAP, establishing the WIC Program, Women's Infants and Children Program, expanding school nutrition programs. And we made progress in the 1970s trying to eradicate hunger. And then in the 1980s, we began to backslide. In the 1990s, we did. And then here we are today with 40 million people who don't know where the next meal is going to come from. This really is about political will and about making this a priority issue. Around the world, and that's where the Montgomery Door Program is, is helping establish school meals in the poorest countries in the world. It is an enticement for poor families to send their kids to school so they can learn to read and write. We find that families in poor countries are more likely to send their daughters to school, which is really important, because women tend to be leaders of family units in poor countries. So there's a benefit as well to the McGovern-Dole program. I also think if people are moved by that, there's also a national security argument to be made.
